newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Marketing seen key to Australian LNG project.
newsitem.headline: Marketing seen key to Australian LNG project.

text.p: Marketing will be the key to success in determining which liquiefied natural gas (LNG) project takes off in Darwin, Australia, energy consultants Wood Mackenzie (Woodmac) said in a report issued on Monday.

The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd of Australia, Phillips Petroleum Co of the United States and a joint venture between Royal Dutch/Shell and Woodside Petroleum of Australia have competing proposals to develop LNG projects onshore and offshore Darwin.
The bigger Woodside/Shell project proposes an onshore plant to generate 7.5 million tonnes of LNG a year from 2005 onwards.
The BHP and Phillips plans target plants with capacity of up to three million tonnes per year, starting production around 2003.
Both BHP and Phillips would feed off the Bayu/Undan field in the Australia/Indonesia zone of cooperation in the Timor Sea.
British-based Woodmac said in a report the Woodside/Shell plant was looking to big volume buyers of LNG, like Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, for potential sales.

"However, the size of the facility means that the project will be competing on the world stage with other large LNG projects which are targeting the same window of opportunity into these markets," it said.
"By contrast, the medium scale facility design of Bayu/Undan allows for the opportunity to target smaller, emerging markets such as India, Philippines, Thailand and China.

"In addition, it is conceivable that medium scale LNG projects can also target the larger markets by filling the gaps which are created by the step-by-step start-up of the large LNG schemes," the report said.
BHP and Phillips are joint venture partners in the Bayu/Undan gas field but they differ over the best approach for building an LNG plant.
BHP wants to build offshore Darwin -- which would be a world first.
Phillips favours an onshore plant using the company's own proprietary technology. It would require a 470 km (294 mile) pipeline from the field.
But Woodmac said that if support for the Woodside/Shell proposal gathered pace, "then it seems inevitable that Bayu/Undan would become part of this greater" plan.
The Woodside/Shell plant would be underpinned by gas reserves from Shell's Sunrise and Troubador fields in the Timor Sea.
But the plant would have to call on addition reserves to fulfill its proposed 7.5 million tonnes per year production base.
